title: Sugriva and Vali
hookLine: two monkey brothers, a sealed cave, and the arrow Hindus still argue about
carry: dharma is subtle; even rama's gets questioned
tomorrow: an army at last. so why does everything stop?
last: BHAV: GOD IS HUNGRY FOR LOVE.

lines: VALI CHASES A DEMON INTO A CAVE.
SUGRIVA SEALS IT, THINKING HIM DEAD.
cards: Two brothers. The older one, Vali, is king of the monkeys, enormously strong. One night a demon challenges him and runs into a cave, and Vali chases him in, telling his younger brother Sugriva to wait at the entrance.
Sugriva waits. A whole year. Then blood pours out of the cave, and he's sure his brother is dead.
So he rolls a boulder over the entrance, goes home, and, at the kingdom's urging, becomes king. Then Vali walks out. Alive, and victorious.
And the first thing he sees is a rock sealing him in and his little brother on his throne.

teach.b: Vali doesn't believe it was a mistake. He drives Sugriva out and takes his wife as well. Sugriva hides on a mountain with Hanuman and a few friends.
There Rama and Lakshmana find him. Two exiles, each wronged. They make a pact over a fire: Rama will help Sugriva win back his kingdom, and Sugriva's monkey army will help find Sita.
Sugriva challenges Vali while Rama waits behind the trees. But the brothers look alike, and Sugriva is beaten badly.

teach.h: THE SHOT FROM BEHIND THE TREES.
teach.b: The second time, Sugriva wears a garland of flowers, and from behind the trees, Rama shoots Vali. Vali falls, furious, with a point. You shot me from hiding, he says.
I wasn't even fighting you. Rama answers that Vali took his brother's wife while his brother lived, and that the land is under Bharata's rule, which Rama is bound to uphold.
Vali, dying, accepts it, and asks Rama to look after his son Angada. Hindus have argued about this arrow for centuries. Some say Rama upheld dharma and kept his word to an ally.
Others say it's the act in his story that doesn't sit right.

teach.h: VALI MAKES HIS CASE, OUT LOUD.
teach.b: And the Ramayana itself lets Vali make his case out loud. That's a teaching too.
In Valmiki, Rama himself tells Vali that dharma is subtle and hard to know.
Right and wrong aren't always on the surface, so Hindus are expected to weigh and ask, even about God's own avatar. Questioning this arrow isn't disloyal. It's what the tradition does.
When your family argues about what was right, the story says: argue honestly, and let the other side speak.

how: The killing of Vali is one of the Ramayana episodes Hindu teachers and commentators debate openly; in temple talks, in Ramlila, and in classical commentaries it is taught alongside Vali's objection and Rama's answer, often with the reminder that dharma is subtle.

games.q: match the story to the teaching.
p: chased a demon into a cave
sealed the cave, thinking him dead

s: Sugriva sealed the cave to trap his brother
in the story he thought Vali was dead. it was a mistake Vali never believed.
Vali gets to argue that the shot was unfair
the Ramayana lets him make his case out loud before Rama answers.
Hindus aren't supposed to question Rama
Hindu teachers have debated the Vali arrow for centuries, and the Ramayana gives Vali his say.

games.q: at dinner, one uncle says Rama was right to shoot Vali; another says it was wrong. everyone looks at you. what does the tradition itself do?
o: declare a winner and end it.
let both make their case: dharma is subtle, and the Ramayana lets Vali speak.
change the subject. you can't question Rama.
games.why: the Ramayana puts Vali's objection and Rama's answer side by side, and Hindus have argued it ever since. dharma is subtle.

practice: Bring to mind a fight between two people you love, and don't pick a side yet. Do what the Ramayana does for Vali: say the other side's best case out loud, in their words, as fairly as you can. Then say your own.
Notice what you understand now that you didn't a minute ago.

wordCard.voice: Sugriva, the good-necked one: the younger brother who sealed Vali in a cave by mistake, restored by an arrow people still argue about.

orig.note: Sanskrit: su (good, beautiful) + griva (neck). Sugriva, the one with the handsome neck.

carryVoice: Carry this: dharma is subtle, and even Rama's gets questioned. Vali got to make his case, too. Day fifty-five, done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (the pact; the seven sala trees; the two duels; Vali's death and his objection, roughly sargas 5–18)

'dharma is subtle': Rama's own words to the dying Vali in Kishkindha Kanda (the dharma of the good is subtle and hard to know, roughly sarga 18), and a principle repeated in the Mahabharata; paraphrased, not quoted
